ety.text: From a merger of two words: * Middle English shutel, shotel, schetel, schettell, schyttyl, scutel (“bar; bolt”), from Old English sċyttel, sċutel (“bar; bolt”), equivalent to shut + -le * Middle English shutel, schetil, shotil, shetel, schootyll, shutyll, schytle, scytyl (“missile; projectile; spear”), from Old English sċytel, sċutel (“dart, arrow”), from Proto-Germanic *skutilaz. The name for a loom weaving instrument, recorded from 1338, is from a sense of being "shot" across the threads.

senses.d: A tool used to carry the woof back and forth between the warp threads on a loom.
ex: My dayes are ſwifter then a weauers ſhuttle, and are ſpent without hope.

Like shuttles through the loom, so swiftly glide
My feather'd hours, and all my hopes deride!.

senses.d: The sliding thread holder in a sewing machine, which carries the lower thread through a loop of the upper thread, to make a lock stitch.
A transport service (such as a bus or train) that goes back and forth between two or more places.
ex: The shuttle bus runs to the airport on a half-hourly basis from the central station.

senses.d: Such a transport vehicle; a shuttle bus; a space shuttle.
Any other item that moves repeatedly back and forth between two positions, possibly transporting something else with it between those points (such as, in chemistry, a molecular shuttle).
A shuttlecock.
A shutter, as for a channel for molten metal.
To go or send back and forth between two places.
To transport by shuttle or by means of a shuttle service.
ex: Guests can be shuttled to and from the hotel for no extra cost.

grp.label: the sliding thread holder in a sewing machine

Borrowed from French navette.
From spola (“spool”) + -etta (diminutive suffix).
From lanzar + -dera.
Borrowed from French navette.

ety.text: From Middle English schitten, schetten, from Old English sċyttan (“to cause rapid movement, shoot a bolt, shut, bolt”), from Proto-West Germanic *skuttjan, from Proto-Germanic *skutjaną, *skuttijaną (“to bar, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *skuttą, *skuttjō (“bar, bolt, shed”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to drive, fall upon, rush”). The Modern English word was originally a dialect form; the Old English word would have normally merged with shit.
Variation of chute or shute (archaic, related to shoot) from Old English scēotan.

senses.d: To remove or block an opening, gap or passage through.
ex: Please shut the door.
The light was so bright I had to shut my eyes.

senses.d: To make or become unreceptive.
ex: He has shut his mind to new ideas.

senses.d: To close (a business or venue) temporarily or permanently.
ex: They generally shut the museum each day at 6 pm.
The supermarket shuts at eight o'clock.

senses.d: To put out of use or operation.
ex: We are shutting the phone lines at 9 pm.
They shut the airport because of a bomb scare.

senses.d: To cease operation or cease to be available.
ex: Phone lines will shut in ten minutes.

senses.d: To terminate an application, window, file or database connection, etc.
ex: Shut the file when you have finished reading data.
This app has a bug: when you try to sort a large spreadsheet, it shuts.

senses.d: To catch or snag in the act of shutting something.
ex: He's just gone and shut his finger in the door!

senses.d: To confine in an enclosed area; to enclose.
ex: I shut the cat in the kitchen before going out.

senses.d: To isolate, to close off from the world.
To preclude, exclude.
ex: shut from every shore

senses.d: Physically sealed, obstructed, folded together, etc.
ex: A shut door barred our way into the house.
The door banged shut with a breeze.

senses.d: Not available for use or operation.
ex: Phone lines are now shut.

senses.d: Not operating or conducting trade; not allowing entrance to visitors or the public.
ex: Banks are shut on bank holidays.
The museum is shut for the Christmas holidays.

senses.d: Not receptive.
ex: He mind is shut to new ideas.

senses.d: Of a club, bat or other hitting implement, angled downwards and/or (for a right-hander) anticlockwise of straight.
Synonym of close.
Synonym of close.
The act or time of shutting; close.
ex: the shut of a door
Just then returnd at ſhut of Evening Flours.

senses.d: A door or cover; a shutter.
The line or place where two pieces of metal are welded together.
A narrow alley or passage acting as a short cut through the buildings between two streets.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French fermer (“to close”), Latin firmāre (“make firm, confirm”).
Inherited from Latin clūdere, variant of claudere.
From Vulgar Latin *serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“to fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, cross-bar”).
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, cross-bar”). Compare English serry/serried.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fechar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin pesclum, from Latin pessulus (“bolt”). Probably a southern Portuguese variant, with the change of /p/ to /f/ reflecting Arabic influence. By surface analysis, fecho + -ar.
Originally the same word as scuffle, and properly a frequentative of shove.

senses.d: The act of mixing cards or mah-jong tiles so as to randomize them.
ex: He made a real mess of the last shuffle.

senses.d: The act of reordering anything, such as music tracks in a media player.
An instance of walking without lifting one's feet.
ex: The sad young girl left with a tired shuffle.

senses.d: A rhythm commonly used in blues music, consisting of a series of triplet notes with the middle note missing, so that it sounds like a long note followed by a short note, and suggests a walker dragging one foot.
A dance move in which the foot is scuffed back and forth across the floor.
A trick; an artifice; an evasion.
ex: The Gifts of Nature are beyond all the Shams and Shuffles in the World.

senses.d: To put in a random order.
ex: Don't forget to shuffle the cards.
You shuffle, and I'll deal.

senses.d: To change; modify the order of something.
To move in a slovenly, dragging manner; to drag or scrape the feet in walking or dancing.
ex: He shuffled out of the room.
I shuffled my feet in embarrassment.

senses.d: To change one's position; to shift ground; to evade questions; to resort to equivocation; to prevaricate.
ex: I myself, […] hiding mine honour in my necessity, am fain to shuffle.

senses.d: To use arts or expedients; to make shift.
ex: Your life, good master, / Must shuffle for itself.

senses.d: To shove one way and the other; to push from one to another.
ex: to shuffle money from hand to hand

senses.d: To remove or introduce by artificial confusion.

to walk without picking up one's feet

es:barajar.gl: to shuffle (to put in random order)

ety.text: From shut + -er. Compare shuttle.

senses.d: One who shuts or closes something.
ex: the openers and shutters of the sluices we believe are basic to the history of mind
The volunteers consisted of a ringmaster, two experienced young cattlemen to grade the cattle, gate-openers and shutters[…]

senses.d: Each of a series of protective panels, usually wooden, placed over windows to block out the light.
A similar screen used as an improvised stretcher to carry someone wounded or sick.
ex: [T]he other fiddler had been carried home, exhausted, on a shutter.
‘I can remember his body coming home, on a shutter I suppose, just as I was going down to tea […].’

senses.d: The part of a camera, normally closed, that opens for a controlled period of time to let light in when taking a picture.
Any other opening and closing device.
A panel used to contain freshly poured concrete, which is usually removed when the concrete hardens.
ex: The vertical wall was poured in two lifts, using two pairs of steel shutters which were bolted tightly onto 9-in. long wooden spacers.

senses.d: To close shutters covering.
ex: Shutter the windows: there's a storm coming!

senses.d: To close up (a building) for a prolonged period of inoccupancy.
ex: It took all day to shutter the cabin now that the season has ended.

senses.d: To cancel or terminate.
ex: The US is seeking to get Iran to shutter its nuclear weapons program.
This company was shuttered in 2002.

senses.d: To rain heavily.
ex: It's a bastard of a day, shuttering rain, but I can still shape up the hills off in the distance.

senses.d: The action of stopping operations; a closing, of a computer, business, event, etc.
ex: You need to enter your password at startup, but it's not required at shutdown.
There is a plastic molly-guard covering the escalator's shutdown button to prevent little kids from pushing it and stopping the escalator.

senses.d: A statement, insult, etc. that prevents the opponent from replying further.
ex: When he insulted me, my reply was such a shutdown that he left the room.

senses.d: An autistic response to stress or sensory overload, in which the individual freezes up and becomes silent, motionless, and unresponsive.
ex: I retreated into myself and allowed myself to be swallowed into a typically autistic shutdown.
I may even reach the point where I have an autistic shutdown, which means I'll be unable to communicate, interact or socialize.

senses.d: A defensive ploy that prevents the opposing players from attacking.
A big success; a hyped atmosphere.
ex: Fashion week and it's shutdown / Went to the show, sitting in the front row / In a black tracksuit and it's shutdown
